Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a prompt for checking the English subtitle file for Mira Vale’s concert at North Pier Hall on 14 June 2024. the file is called `mira_vale_north_pier_2024-06-14_en.srt` and it covers the full 82-minute recording. this is for the community archive upload, and there is no second subtitle file or transcript to compare against, so the prompt should work from that file alone. i want a careful pass, not a new translation and not a rewritten version of the show. The file includes song lyrics, short spoken introductions, audience reactions and a few announcements from the hall. They all belong in the file. Please make the request clear that the person checking it should not remove a cue just because it is brief, repetitive, or mostly a crowd response. The archive coordinator told me, “Please keep the crowd responses where they are; people use them to line up the recording.” That matters especially during the pause after the first set, when the room noise is subtitled too.

The main thing I’m hoping for is a modest spelling and punctuation check of the subtitle wording, but only if the file is structurally usable. Before touching the words, check the cue blocks. Each block needs a cue number, a timestamp line in the usual SRT form, a start and end time that make sense, and subtitle text. Cue numbers should move forward in order; the timings should move forward too and shouldn’t overlap. I mean every block in the file, not just the first page or the song sections. If all of those checks pass for the entire file, then do the wording pass. If one or more don’t pass, don’t start correcting the wording; that would make it hard to tell what happened to a broken file. I keep saying this because the word check is the main job only after that condition is met, not a general instruction to clean up whatever is there.

For the wording pass, stick to clear spelling errors and punctuation that is missing or plainly wrong. Please don’t smooth out Mira’s phrasing, make informal speech sound formal, or replace a line with a neater sentence. This is a live performance and the wording should continue to sound like what people said. Don’t fill in a lyric that seems to be missing, guess at words hidden by noise, or change a line because another phrasing sounds more likely. There is no other transcript for checking against. Names and song titles should remain as they appear in the source, including “Paper Lanterns,” “A Map of Rain,” and “Last Ferry Home.” Don’t decide that a title or a repeated lyric is a spelling mistake just because it appears more than once. The set list is not a source of permission to alter the sung lines.

Also keep the existing cue order, cue numbers, timestamps, and boundaries exactly where they are. Don’t combine two cues, split a cue, move a response earlier or later, or change the amount of time a subtitle is on screen. Keep the words in their current cue, including the audience responses that follow the songs. There are speaker labels such as MIRA and AUDIENCE in the file; retain the labels and their placement. If punctuation can be corrected without changing the words or moving anything, that is fine, but don’t make a subtitle more descriptive or add stage directions. The file already has the material it is meant to contain, and this request is for a limited check rather than a content expansion.

There are a couple of places that might tempt someone to over-edit. Mira introduces “A Map of Rain” with a short story about a ferry, and the audience calls out during the ending of “Last Ferry Home.” Leave those lines in the form they have in the file except for the narrow spelling and punctuation check if the structural condition passes. The hall announcement before the encore is part of the recording too, even though it is not Mira speaking. Don’t discard it or attribute it to her. I’m not asking for a summary, an explanation of the songs, a new subtitle style, or a review of the performance. Please keep this focused on the supplied English SRT, and don’t consult or invent a different version of what anyone said.

If the structural check fails anywhere, the useful alternative is a concise list of the cue numbers with the structural problem for each one, rather than an attempted wording edit. Say what is wrong in practical terms, such as a missing number, an invalid timestamp line, a start time that does not precede its end time, a timing that goes backward or overlaps the previous cue, or a block with no subtitle text. Only report issues that actually appear in the file; don’t guess at missing content or propose replacement timings. If there are several faults in one cue, it can be one entry for that cue. The purpose of that alternative is to let the archive team locate the affected blocks before anyone does a text pass.

The output needs to be usable without an accompanying note. If the condition passes, return only the corrected SRT text, retaining its cue structure and all untouched material. If the condition does not pass, return only the concise cue-number issue list instead, and do not include a corrected file as well. No preface, sign-off, general assessment, or extra recommendation. Keep the two possible outputs separate: the spelling and punctuation check is allowed only when every structural check succeeds, and the issue list is the fallback otherwise. ## 1. Check the file structure first

Before editing any wording, check every cue block in the entire file. Confirm that each block has a cue number, a timestamp line in the usual SRT form, a valid start and end time, and subtitle text. Cue numbers and timings must move forward in order, and cues must not overlap.

Proceed to the wording check only if every structural check passes for the whole file. If any check fails, do not edit the wording; use the fallback output described below instead.

## 2. Limited wording check, if the structure passes

Correct only clear spelling errors and missing or plainly incorrect punctuation. Keep the wording faithful to the live performance. Do not smooth Mira’s phrasing, formalize informal speech, rewrite lines, fill in missing lyrics, guess words obscured by noise, or substitute a more likely-sounding phrase. Do not use the set list to alter sung lines. Retain names and song titles as they appear in the source, including “Paper Lanterns,” “A Map of Rain,” and “Last Ferry Home.” Do not treat repeated titles or lyrics as errors merely because they recur.

Keep every cue number, timestamp, boundary, and position unchanged. Do not combine or split cues, move subtitles, or change their on-screen duration. Leave each line in its current cue, including audience responses after songs. Retain speaker labels such as MIRA and AUDIENCE in their existing positions. Do not add descriptions or stage directions.

Keep all existing material: song lyrics, spoken introductions, audience reactions, the room-noise subtitle during the pause after the first set, and the hall announcement before the encore. The announcement is not Mira speaking; do not remove it or attribute it to her. In particular, leave the ferry story introducing “A Map of Rain” and the audience calls during the ending of “Last Ferry Home” in their existing form, apart from the permitted spelling and punctuation corrections. The archive coordinator said, “Please keep the crowd responses where they are; people use them to line up the recording.”

## 3. Fallback if any structural check fails

Do not perform a wording edit. Return a concise list of the cue numbers with structural problems, stating the practical issue for each cue. Possible issues include a missing number, invalid timestamp line, start time that does not precede the end time, timing that goes backward or overlaps the previous cue, or missing subtitle text. Report only problems present in the file. Do not guess missing content or propose replacement timings. If one cue has several faults, one entry for that cue is sufficient.

## Output

Return only one of these, as appropriate:

- If every structural check passes: the corrected SRT text, preserving its cue structure and all untouched material.
- If any structural check fails: the concise cue-number issue list, without a corrected file.

Do not include a preface, sign-off, general assessment, explanation of the songs, performance review, style redesign, summary, or recommendation."}]
